summary:
AXIAL-98, developed by Team Uranuß, helps astronauts and flight surgeons stay connected to health data—even when deep-space missions lose contact with Earth.

The system pairs a sensor-equipped undersuit and smartwatch with a web app that has two views: a network simulator and an Astronaut Health Console. Wearables track key health indicators such as heart rate, oxygen levels, sleep, mood, and movement, alongside habitat conditions like carbon dioxide, noise, and radiation.

When the connection to Earth is delayed or lost, AXIAL-98 stores health updates on board and sorts them by urgency. Astronauts can still receive procedural guidance, and the system sends queued updates to flight surgeons when communication returns. This store-and-forward approach is designed for missions to the ISS, the Moon, and Mars.
details:
What it does and how it works

AXIAL-98 connects astronaut health wearables with onboard mission software and ground-based medical teams. It has three main parts:

  1. Wearables and habitat sensors
    A smartwatch tracks signals such as pulse, skin temperature, movement, and stress-related activity. A sensor-equipped undersuit monitors heart and breathing signals, while suit and habitat sensors measure conditions such as carbon dioxide, oxygen, air pressure, and radiation.
  2. Store-and-forward telemetry
    The network simulator in astra_demo.html models communication on the ISS, at a lunar base, and during a Mars transit. Users can adjust latency, add packet loss, or cut either communication link. When a link is down, health records are saved locally and sorted by urgency: Urgent Crew Reports, Mission Priority, and Routine. The system retries delivery when the connection returns.
  3. Astronaut Health Console
    In astronot-saglik-v2.html, astronauts can review body-mapped indicators, charts, and procedural checklists. The console is designed to support approved onboard procedures without making automated medical diagnoses.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Health records can survive communication outages. AXIAL-98 queues critical updates during blackouts and sends them when a connection is available.
  • Health and environmental data stay distinct. The system separates readings such as carbon dioxide and radiation from biometric data and crew-reported symptoms. It can present approved guidance onboard while leaving clinical decisions to flight surgeons.

Tools, hardware, and software

  • Software: HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript, with local storage, priority-based queueing, and a URL-based data bridge.
  • Hardware concept: The proposed flight architecture uses radiation-hardened VORAGO VA41630 or Microchip SAMRH71 microcontrollers with Analog Devices sensor front ends, including the ADPD4100 and MAX30001. An ESP32/Wokwi hardware twin and 3D concepts for the smartwatch and compression undersuit support prototyping.
